item.title: This American Life: 436: The Psychopath Test
item.description:
We heard about a test that could determine if someone was a psychopath. So, naturally, our staff decided to take it. 

Become a This American Life Partner to listen ad-free and receive regular bonus episodes.

(00:00:00) Prologue: When the staff of the show decided to take a psychopathy test, everyone agreed that the highest score would go to one of three people: Robyn, Jane, or Ira. (6 minutes)

(00:06:36) Act One: Alix Spiegel tells the story of Robert Dixon, an inmate at a maximum-security prison in Vacaville, California. He’s unlikely ever to be paroled because of his score on a psychopathy test. Alix traces how the test was created and learns that its creator, Bob Hare, is troubled by how it’s used in the criminal justice system today. (28 minutes)

(00:34:21) Act Two: Jon Ronson looks into whether psychopaths are more common in the corporate world. To find out, he visits Al Dunlap, the former CEO of Sunbeam, who was known for cutting thousands of jobs. (15 minutes)

(00:51:12) Act Three: Ira and the staff get their psychopath test results from Dr. David Bernstein, a forensic psychologist with Forensic Consultants, who gave them the test. (6 minutes)

Transcripts are available at thisamericanlife.org / This American Life privacy policy. / Learn more about sponsor message choices.

item.title: People I (Mostly) Admire: 49. Mathematician Sarah Hart on Why Numbers are Music to Our Ears
item.description:

Sarah, a professor at the University of London and Gresham College, also talks with Steve about the gender gap in mathematics and why being interested in everything can be a problem. item.title: Radiolab: Terminal Delirium
item.description:
When producer Alan Goffinski's dad called him and said he only had a few months left to live, Alan rushed home to spend one last Christmas with him. What happened when he got there shocked him, completely upended what he thinks about how people die, and sent him on a reporting journey into the depths of the human mind and soul.

Special thanks to Pam and Curtis Goffinski, Travis Thatcher, Sam Brudner and Elizabeth Deerhake.

item.title: Freakonomics Radio: 696. Build, Baby, Build!
item.description:
Why is there such a shortage of family-friendly housing? Land-use and environmental regulations have a lot to do with it. We hear how Austin has been rewriting the rules — and ask whether other cities could do the same. (Part two of a two-part series.)

 

  • SOURCES:
    • Nick Bloom, professor of economics at Stanford University.
    • Ed Glaeser, professor of economics at Harvard University.
    • Kathy Hochul, governor of New York.
    • Melissa Kearney, professor of economics at the University of Notre Dame.
    • Lyman Stone, director of the Pronatalism Initiative at the Institute for Family Studies.
    • Kirk Watson, mayor of Austin, Texas.

 

  • RESOURCES:
    • "Austin’s Surge of New Housing Construction Drove Down Rents," by Liz Clifford, Seva Rodnyansky, and Dennis Su (Pew Research Center, 2026).
    • "Inequality, not regulation, drives America's housing affordability crisis," by Maximilian Buchholz, Tom Kemeny, Gregory F. Randol

item.title: Ignited: Striking Industrial Automation Conversations: Built to Impress: Inside Two of ICC 2026's Most Innovative Ignition Projects
item.description:
Recorded live on-site at ICC 2026 in Sacramento, Travis and Tom sit down with two of the engineers behind two of this year's standout Discover Gallery projects. First, Greg Schneider from Multi-Dimensional Integration shares how his team used RFID tracking and Ignition's Event Streams module to bring a 100-year-old Pittsburgh bakery into digital BRCGS food safety certification. Then, Pat Smith from Avadine explains how they replaced a siloed legacy monitoring system for Magnolia Oil & Gas with iPOC—an Ignition-native solution bringing 800 pump-off controller wells into their existing SCADA environment.

Guests:

  • Greg Schneider (Senior Engineer, Multi-Dimensional Integration)
  • Pat Smith (Director of Technical Solutions, Avadine)

item.title: Planet Money: Two ways big bets on data centers might affect you (Two Indicators)
item.description:
Your money might be fueling the AI boom … just as some AI data center bets are starting to look riskier. If you own stocks, that money is likely tied up in giant tech companies like Microsoft and Nvidia. And if your 401(k) has money invested in the US bond fund, you might be lending tech companies the money to build data centers. 

Today on the show, two stories from our short daily podcast The Indicator from Planet Money on how risky these data center bets are for investors and the companies making them. And, of course, for all of us.

item.title: What We Spend: To Move Or Not to Move?
item.description:
Sadie is a single mom raising her 14-year-old daughter in Ohio, in the same house she grew up in herself. Now, she’s thinking about moving to Portugal, where her grandparents immigrated from. The thing is – she’s never been there. We’ll follow Sadie as she considers whether to leave behind the only home she’s ever known for a chance at a completely different life.
